entries.title: Man runs red light, causes two buses to crash: police
entries.summary: <p>A bus driver was in critical condition and at least eight other people were hospitalized after a driver ran a red light and caused two CTA buses to crash in East Garfield Park Wednesday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>A man driving a sedan eastbound on West Lake Street at 6:42 p.m. drove through a red light and hit a CTA bus going south on South Homan Avenue, which then hit another CTA bus going north on Homan, police said. The driver of the second CTA bus was taken to Stroger Hospital in critical condition.</p><p>The driver of the sedan was issued several citations and also taken to Stroger Hospital, in stable condition, police said. Seven bus passengers also were taken to local hospitals in various conditions.</p><p>The CTA didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.</p>

entries.title: Teen charged in fatal Back of the Yards shooting
entries.summary: <p>A teen was arrested and charged Tuesday in the fatal shooting of a man in Back of the Yards last August, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The 17-year-old faces a charge of first-degree murder, police said. He was arrested in Hickory Hills on Tuesday.</p><p>David Carmona, 20, was arguing with someone in the 4700 block of South Damen Avenue when he turned to walk away, and other person allegedly shot him in the buttocks, police said. Carmona was taken in critical condition to Stroger Hospital, where he later died.</p>

entries.title: Marina Mabrey and the Sky still see the best in each other
entries.summary: <p>There are many ways to identify former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> guard Marina Mabrey. She's a middle child. One of the best players in the league to have never been named an All-Star. Inventor of the "Crash-Out Jar," a running joke in which she deposited dollars after losing her temper in games.</p><p></p><p>Now, add "face of the franchise" to the list.</p><p></p><p>The Tempo signed her to a two-year max contract this past offseason, making her and Brittney Sykes the faces of the league's first Canadian team.</p><p></p><p>She led the Tempo to an 111-104 win over the Sky Wednesday night, scoring 23 points on 9-13 from the field — and almost immediately reminding fans that the Mabrey experience contains multitudes.</p><p></p><p>Step-back threes. Incredulous conversations with the officials. Perfectly-timed floaters. Poorly-timed fouls.</p><p></p><p>Mabrey's brief tenure with the Sky contained multitudes too. She set the single-season record for three pointers in 2023 (81) and grew her game in 2024. But<b> </b>her stint ended in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky-and-wnba/2024/07/19/marina-mabreys-trade-request-came-with-a-desire-to-play-for-sun" target="_blank" >a request to be traded</a>from the Sky to the Sun midway through the 2024 season. At shootaround before the game, she reflected on how those experiences shaped her.</p><p></p><p>"I've been in leadership positions in Chicago and Connecticut where there were some things I still needed to learn, and I'm still learning right now, but I think that I took those things and put it into this team," Mabrey told the Sun-Times.</p><p></p><p>"I think finding a home helps a lot too. I've jumped around trying to find a situation that works for me and my vision for myself."</p><p></p><p>The Tempo are Mabrey’s fourth team in six years. She's moved from Dallas to Chicago to Connecticut, now to Toronto, all before the age of 30.</p><p></p><p>Few have cycled through as many situations as Mabrey has. Except, perhaps, for the Sky.</p><p></p><p>Mabrey saw the organizational chaos firsthand, living through the peak instability of Chicago's post-2021 championship era. Coach and general manager James Wade, who brought her to Chicago, left in the middle of the 2023 season. Then franchise pillar Kahleah Copper requested a trade.</p><p></p><p>The lesson she took was about staying true to herself.</p><p></p><p>"I think knowing that people will come in and out of organizations, you will have different people to work with, but keeping the vision for yourself that you know is you," she said. "Regardless of who you're playing around, who's coming in, who's not coming in, who's leaving.</p><p></p><p>"I think for me, I maybe lost myself a little bit in Chicago, in trying to figure out who I was alongside everyone. ... I lost the vision of who I know I can be."</p><p></p><p>According to Sykes, who has played against Mabrey since childhood, her vision is to become an offensive juggernaut — but one who has learned to wield her emotions rather than be consumed by them.</p><p></p><p>That's something Tempo coach Sandy Brondello, a two-time WNBA champion, is trying to facilitate.</p><p></p><p>"She's actually quite funny," Brondello said of Mabrey. "Now, if she crashes out, it's usually at the officials. It's never at her teammates, which is a good thing. Now it's more like, 'Just don't get too high or too low.'</p><p></p><p>"But that's her edge. You don't want to change someone. That's her competitive fire. But not letting it affect her overall game."</p><p></p><p>Mabrey only played in Chicago from 2023-2024, but she left a mark on the organization. She embodies two of their defining characteristics: a willingness to risk draft capital to win now, and a spotty track record in retaining stars.</p><p></p><p>To acquire her from the Wings, Wade traded away a staggering amount of draft capital: a 2023 first-rounder, a 2024 first-rounder and a 2025 pick swap.</p><p></p><p>It set the tone for a philosophy that current general manager Jeff Pagliocca has maintained. In Chicago, there will be no tanking, no waiting to strike gold in the draft lottery. Every year it's trying to bring in the best players through trades and free agency, at pretty much whatever cost.</p><p></p><p>So far, the strategy hasn't yielded a ton of tangible success — the Sky have missed the postseason the last two years — but it also hasn't backfired to the proportions one might have imagined.</p><p></p><p>The Mabrey deal is a perfect example. The 2023 pick the Sky surrendered ultimately became a worthless late first-rounder, and the 2025 swap was canceled entirely when the Wings won the No. 1 pick on their own. Had the Sky been able to retain Mabrey, the trade could have aged as a win.</p><p></p><p>She is now producing at the level Wade likely envisioned — 18.8 points per game — and that current coach Tyler Marsh respects.</p><p></p><p>His keys for success against the Tempo revolved around keeping Mabrey in vision at all times, given how quickly she gets off her shot.</p><p></p><p>"I'm a big fan of Marina, the toughness and competitiveness that she plays with — you accept some other stuff that comes with it," Marsh said. "I remember when we played Connecticut last year and I got thrown out of that game, I saw Marina after the game, I said, 'I pulled a you tonight.'"</p><p></p><p>The respect goes both ways.</p><p></p><p>Mabrey is genuinely impressed with the direction the Sky roster has gone. She said at shootaround that Pagliocca has built a tougher and more talented roster — two of his primary goals.</p><p></p><p>Despite all the turbulence, it appears both sides can still see the best in each other.</p>

entries.title: DOJ investigation referred E. Jean Carroll for prosecution in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>The Justice Department earlier this year referred an investigation into E. Jean Carroll, the longtime advice columnist who accused President Donald Trump of sexual assault, to federal prosecutors in Chicago, a law enforcement source told the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>That investigation is active within U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros’ office, the source said. </p><p>Neither the U.S. Department of Justice nor Boutros' office immediately responded to requests for comment Wednesday night. The story was first reported by <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/05/27/politics/exclusive-justice-department-launched-e-jean-carroll-investigation" target="_blank" ><u>CNN</u></a>.</p><p>Prosecutors are focused on a 2022 deposition by Carroll in which she said she received no outside funding for her legal action against Trump, though it was later revealed that billionaire LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman had chipped in for some legal fees and expenses, CNN reported. Hoffman has a nonprofit based in Chicago.</p><p>In January 2024, as Trump closed in on the Republican presidential nomination, a jury awarded $83.3 million to Carroll in that same suit for Trump’s continued social media attacks against her over her <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/6/21/18701574/e-jean-carroll-donald-trump-rape" target="_blank" ><u>claims that he sexually assaulted her</u></a> in a Manhattan department store. That total includes a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/5/9/23717528/jury-finds-trump-liable-for-sexual-abuse-awards-accuser-e-jean-carroll-5-million" target="_blank" ><u>$5 million sexual abuse and defamation verdict</u></a> in May 2023 she was awarded by another jury.</p><p>The jury that issued the May 2023 verdict rejected Carroll’s claim that she was raped, finding Trump responsible for a lesser degree of sexual abuse. The judgment offered vindication to Carroll, whose allegations had been mocked and dismissed by Trump for years.</p><p>Trump has since appealed the awards multiple times, including to the Supreme Court, which has <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-carroll-abuse-defamation-670dd7ed241e22c52bd16e82a9febf69" target="_blank" ><u>repeatedly rejected</u></a> the president’s requests to hear the case.</p><p>It comes at a time when Boutros’ office is embroiled in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/27/broadview-six-boutros-kat-abughazaleh-ice-trump-chicago-broadview" target="_blank" ><u>biggest credibility crisis it has faced in recent memory</u></a>.</p><p>The “Broadview Six” case against six Operation Midway Blitz protesters <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" ><u>fell apart days before trial</u></a> after a judge discovered improprieties during grand jury proceedings.</p><p>The alleged misconduct by prosecutors came to light only after a lengthy push by defense attorneys to get the judge to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/04/broadview-six-grand-jury-transcript-conspiracy" target="_blank" ><u>review unredacted transcripts</u></a> of what occurred, and shockwaves from the case have begun to reach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/27/broadview-six-boutros-kat-abughazaleh-ice-trump-chicago-broadview" target="_blank" ><u>courts outside of Illinois</u></a>.</p><p><i>Contributing: AP</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" courtroom</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Twins manager Derek Shelton not surprised by White Sox' strong play
entries.summary: <p><b>Derek Shelton</b>, who grew up in north suburban Gurnee, is grateful for a second chance to manage in the majors with the Twins. And he’s with another club that plays in the same division as a Chicago team.</p><p>Starting in 2020, Shelton spent five-plus seasons guiding the Pirates — one of the Cubs’ rivals in the National League Central — until they dismissed him last May after a 12-26 start.</p><p>In his return to the Twins, for whom he was a bench coach in 2018 and 2019, Shelton said he isn’t surprised his team is chasing the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> in the American League Central, even if the South Siders are coming off three seasons with 101 or more losses. After the second-place Sox’ 15-2 rout Wednesday, the Twins trail them by 1½ games.</p><p>‘‘I don’t think it’s surprising at all,’’ Shelton, 55, said of the Sox’ climb. ‘‘I think [general manager] <b>Chris</b> [<b>Getz</b>] and [assistant GM] <b>Josh Barfield</b> and [manager] <b>Will Venable</b> have done an unbelievable job. I mean, they’ve put a plan in place and stuck to that plan.</p><p>‘‘You know, they went out and made really good signings. When you get a first baseman of this caliber [<b>Munetaka Murakami</b>], they got [starter <b>Anthony</b>] <b>Kay</b>, [<b>Colson</b>] <b>Montgomery</b> is a really good player, [<b>Miguel</b>] <b>Vargas</b> they traded for — this is a good baseball team.’’</p><p>In his second managerial job, Shelton said he’s paying attention to detail more than ever.</p><p>‘‘I do think that one of the things that came out of last year was I thought I got away from the attention to detail, what I thought was the attention to detail from my space,’’ he said. ‘‘I wanted to make sure that if I ever did get the next opportunity that I would stay more on top of it and that I would build a staff that stays on top of it.’’</p><p>Shelton was a standout catcher at Warren Township High School, where he was coached by his dad, <b>Ron</b>. He then went on to play at Southern Illinois and in the minors before turning to coaching and, ultimately, managing.</p><p>He said he doesn’t think anyone can be fully prepared for his first managerial job in the majors.</p><p>‘‘The first year you manage, you’re drinking from the fire hose,’’ said Shelton, noting that 2020 was the COVID-shortened season with extra regulations. ‘‘I didn’t know what I was doing.’’</p><h3>Swiss Army knife, made in Japan?</h3><p>Twins left-hander <b>Connor Prielipp</b> started Wednesday, so right-handed-hitting <b>Randal Grichuk</b> took over in right field and batted cleanup, contributing three hits and two RBI in an 18-hit attack. That gave left-handed-hitting newcomer <b>Rikuu Nishida</b> his first day off in the majors after two eventful games.</p><p>Nishida, who played mostly at second base in the minors, admitted that getting used to right field in a major-league stadium presented him with some challenges, even if he made some nifty catches and threw out two runners at the plate.</p><p>Venable said he is confident the 5-6, 150-pound Nishida will excel in right or anywhere else.</p><p>‘‘He’s a baseball player, kind of like [<b>Sam</b>] <b>Antonacci</b>, where you feel like you can throw him anywhere and he’ll make the adjustments and get the job done,’’ Venable said.</p><h3>Hays’ day off</h3><p>Venable said outfielder <b>Austin Hays</b> is being held back by ‘‘lower-body soreness’’ and took Wednesday off during his rehab assignment with Triple-A Charlotte for a strained left calf.</p><p>Hays missed most of April because of a strained right hamstring. He returned April 28 and played three games before hurting his calf May 1 and going on the injured list again.
